claim: The spatial organization of synaptic inputs on the dendritic tree of cortical neurons plays a major role for dendritic integration and neural computations.
source: The spatial organization of synaptic inputs on the dendritic tree of cortical neurons plays a major role for dendritic integration and neural computations, yet, remarkably little is known about it.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of spatial organization, drawing from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Remarkably little is known about the spatial organization of synaptic inputs on the dendritic tree of cortical neurons.
source: The spatial organization of synaptic inputs on the dendritic tree of cortical neurons plays a major role for dendritic integration and neural computations, yet, remarkably little is known about it.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: The synapses of intralaminar inputs form clusters on the basal dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal cells.
source: We found that the synapses of intralaminar inputs form clusters on the basal dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, supported by the CASIM mapping and cluster analysis.

claim: The clusters of intralaminar inputs contain 4 to 14 synapses within ≤30 µm of dendrite.
source: These clusters contain 4 to 14 synapses within ≤30 µm of dendrite.
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of the clusters based on experimental measurements.

claim: The cluster parameters suggest that there will be non-linear dendritic integration of synaptic inputs during synchronous activation.
source: According to the spatiotemporal characteristics of synaptic summation, these numbers suggest that there will be non-linear dendritic integration of synaptic inputs during synchronous activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured cluster parameters and established knowledge about dendritic integration.

claim: Computations on the level of single neurons critically depend on the location and spatial relationship between active synapses.
source: Computations on the level of single neurons critically depend on the location and spatial relationship between active synapses (e.g. Branco and Häusser, 2011; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Polsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Knowing the connectivity of neurons with single synapse resolution is essential to understand how synaptic integration at the cellular level contributes to neural circuit function.
source: Thus knowing the connectivity of neurons with single synapse resolution is essential to understand how synaptic integration at the cellular level contributes to neural circuit function.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the previous statement about the importance of spatial relationships.

claim: Clusters of synaptic inputs can give rise to superlinear summation during synchronous activity.
source: These are clusters of synaptic inputs, which can give rise to superlinear summation during synchronous activity (e.g. DeBello et al., 2014; Larkum and Nevian, 2008; Mel, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Clustering has been reported for synchronously active synapses during spontaneous activity.
source: Clustering has been reported for synchronously active synapses during spontaneous activity (Kleindienst et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2012), for synapses undergoing plasticity (Makino and Malinow, 2011; McBride et al., 2008) as well as for synapses from anatomically defined populations of presynaptic neurons (Druckmann et al., 2014; Rah et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Clustering has been reported for synapses undergoing plasticity.
source: Clustering has been reported for synchronously active synapses during spontaneous activity (Kleindienst et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2012), for synapses undergoing plasticity (Makino and Malinow, 2011; McBride et al., 2008) as well as for synapses from anatomically defined populations of presynaptic neurons (Druckmann et al., 2014; Rah et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Clustering has been reported for synapses from anatomically defined populations of presynaptic neurons.
source: Clustering has been reported for synchronously active synapses during spontaneous activity (Kleindienst et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2012), for synapses undergoing plasticity (Makino and Malinow, 2011; McBride et al., 2008) as well as for synapses from anatomically defined populations of presynaptic neurons (Druckmann et al., 2014; Rah et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cluster parameters relevant for dendritic computations are not rigorously and quantitatively assessed in previous studies.
source: However, the cluster parameters relevant for dendritic computations are not rigorously and quantitatively assessed.
evidence: This is an assertion about the limitations of previous research.

claim: In different cortical areas the patterns of synapses activated by sensory stimulation suggest that inputs onto central neurons may not be clustered.
source: Furthermore, in different cortical areas the patterns of synapses activated by sensory stimulation suggest that inputs onto central neurons may not be clustered (Chen et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2010; Varga et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transgenic mice expressing ChR2-YFP under control of the THY1 promoter (line 18) express ChR2-YFP in L5 pyramidal cells.
source: For presynaptic expression of ChR2, we used transgenic mice expressing ChR2-YFP under control of the THY1 promoter in L5 pyramidal cells (line 18; Wang et al., 2007; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation and reference to a figure.

claim: High photostimulus intensities evoked electrical responses in all probed L5 pyramidal cells.
source: High photostimulus intensities evoked electrical responses in all probed L5 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: An intermediate stimulus intensity evoked action potentials in 58% of L5 pyramidal cells.
source: Because in more sensitive cells the number of generated action potentials dropped with higher stimulus intensities, we applied an intermediate stimulus intensity for synapse mapping, which evoked action potentials in 58% of L5 pyramidal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments, supported by reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Synapses between pairs of L5 pyramidal cells are reported to be located to a large extent on the proximal basal dendrite of the postsynaptic cell.
source: Synapses between pairs of L5 pyramidal cells are reported to be located to a large extend on the proximal basal dendrite of the postsynaptic cell (Markram et al., 1997; Sjoström and Häusser, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Out of 2168 analyzed spines, 199 were L5 input positive (9.2%, n = 20 cells).
source: In total, out of 2168 analyzed spines, 199 were L5 input positive (9.2%, n = 20 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments.

claim: The average peak calcium signal amplitude in successful trials (ΔG/R = 0.48 ± 0.01) was significantly higher than the calcium signal in the parent dendrite (ΔG/R=0.18 ± 0.005, p<0.001, n = 199 spines).
source: The average peak calcium signal amplitude in successful trials (ΔG/R = 0.48 ± 0.01) was significantly higher than the calcium signal in the parent dendrite (ΔG/R=0.18 ± 0.005, p<0.001, n = 199 spines; Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the morphological properties of L5+ spines and L5- spines.
source: There was no significant difference in the morphological properties of L5+ spines and L5 input negative (L5-) spines (length: L5+, 1.23 ± 0.06 μm, n = 76; L5-, 1.11 ± 0.02 μm, n = 419; p=0.04; normalized volume: L5+, 1.00 ± 0.08, n = 77; L5-, 1.00 ± 0.03, n = 437; p=0.97; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: The number of L5+ spines scaled with the total number of probed spines.
source: The number of L5+ spines scaled with the total number of probed spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) but displayed a high degree of heterogeneity between cells (4% to 29%) and individual dendritic segments (3% to 50%) as has been previously reported for Schaffer collateral synapses (Druckmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, supported by reference to a figure and citation.

claim: The number of L5+ spines displayed a high degree of heterogeneity between cells (4% to 29%) and individual dendritic segments (3% to 50%).
source: The number of L5+ spines scaled with the total number of probed spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) but displayed a high degree of heterogeneity between cells (4% to 29%) and individual dendritic segments (3% to 50%) as has been previously reported for Schaffer collateral synapses (Druckmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: High degree of heterogeneity in the number of inputs has been previously reported for Schaffer collateral synapses.
source: The number of L5+ spines scaled with the total number of probed spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) but displayed a high degree of heterogeneity between cells (4% to 29%) and individual dendritic segments (3% to 50%) as has been previously reported for Schaffer collateral synapses (Druckmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The classical analysis of the distribution of pairwise nearest neighbor distances applied to L5+ spines revealed significantly shorter recorded distances than expected from a random distribution.
source: The classical analysis of the distribution of pairwise nearest neighbor distances applied to L5+ spines (e.g. Druckmann et al., 2014; Rah et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2012) revealed significantly shorter recorded distances than expected from a random distribution (Figure 2A), suggesting that L5 inputs are clustered.
evidence: This is a result from data analysis, supported by reference to a figure and citations to methods used in previous studies.

claim: The significantly shorter nearest neighbor distances suggest that L5 inputs are clustered.
source: The classical analysis of the distribution of pairwise nearest neighbor distances applied to L5+ spines (e.g. Druckmann et al., 2014; Rah et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2012) revealed significantly shorter recorded distances than expected from a random distribution (Figure 2A), suggesting that L5 inputs are clustered.
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis results.

claim: 12 clusters of L5+ spines were identified on the basal dendrites of 20 cells.
source: We identified 12 clusters of L5+ spines on the basal dendrites of 20 cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cluster analysis.

claim: The clusters extend over roughly 15 μm with, on average, approximately 8 spines.
source: These clusters extend over roughly 15 μm with, on average, approximately 8 spines (dendritic length, 12.52 ± 2.40 μm; 7.17 ± 0.94 L5+ spines; density, 0.84 ± 0.19 L5+ spines/μm; ratio of L5+ over all spines within the cluster, 0.48 ± 0.04; Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; n = 12 clusters).
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of the clusters from the data.

claim: Almost 50% of all L5+ spines were part of a cluster (86 out of 199).
source: Almost 50% of all L5+ spines were part of a cluster (86 out of 199).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cluster analysis.

claim: Due to the slicing procedure, the size of spine clusters could be underestimated by a factor between 1.4 and 2.
source: There is a possibility, that due to the slicing procedure some inputs may be missed. We estimate that the size of spine clusters could be underestimated by a factor between 1.4 and 2 (see Material and methods; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an estimation based on calculations described in the methods section.

claim: In the cortex, clusters of synapses of an anatomically defined intracortical connection exist, which have the required size and spacing to be relevant for non-linear dendritic computations (≥4 synapses within 30 µm of dendrite).
source: This result shows that in the cortex cluster of synapses of an anatomically defined intracortical connection exist, which have the required size and spacing to be relevant for non-linear dendritic computations (≥4 synapses within 30 µm of dendrite; see e.g. Branco and Häusser, 2011; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Polsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and comparison with established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The scale of these clusters is in line with local learning rules.
source: Furthermore, the scale of these clusters is in line with local learning rules (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Harvey and Svoboda, 2007), which might play a role in cluster formation and furthermore in synapse interactions within the cluster during synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured cluster parameters and cited literature on learning rules.

claim: Local learning rules might play a role in cluster formation and synapse interactions within the cluster during synaptic plasticity.
source: Furthermore, the scale of these clusters is in line with local learning rules (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Harvey and Svoboda, 2007), which might play a role in cluster formation and furthermore in synapse interactions within the cluster during synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Previous studies mapping sensory inputs in different neocortical areas reported no obvious spatial structure in input patterns.
source: Our results are in contrast to previous studies mapping sensory inputs in different neocortical areas, which reported no obvious spatial structure in input patterns and suggested that local non-linear dendritic integration may not be important for sensory processing in the cortex (Chen et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2010; Varga et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies suggested that local non-linear dendritic integration may not be important for sensory processing in the cortex.
source: Our results are in contrast to previous studies mapping sensory inputs in different neocortical areas, which reported no obvious spatial structure in input patterns and suggested that local non-linear dendritic integration may not be important for sensory processing in the cortex (Chen et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2010; Varga et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: More recent studies provided evidence for non-linear computations during cortical processing.
source: However, more recent studies provided evidence for non-linear computations during cortical processing (Lavzin et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A potential explanation for the apparent contradiction is that in the experiments described here, a well-defined set of neurons is stimulated, while inputs defined by the same sensory stimulus are in all likelihood arising from a mix of genetically/anatomically defined types of neurons.
source: A potential explanation for this apparent contradiction (DeBello et al., 2014) is that in the experiments described here, we stimulate a well-defined set of neurons, while inputs which are defined by the same sensory stimulus (Chen et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2010; Varga et al., 2011) are in all likelihood arising from a mix of genetically/anatomically defined types of neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between studies, supported by citations.

claim: Input clustering has been shown for axodendritic contacts in the barn owl auditory system.
source: Input clustering has been shown for axodendritic contacts in the barn owl auditory system (McBride et al., 2008), and more recently, in mice, for thalamocortical (Rah et al., 2013) and hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapses (Druckmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Input clustering has been shown for thalamocortical synapses in mice.
source: Input clustering has been shown for axodendritic contacts in the barn owl auditory system (McBride et al., 2008), and more recently, in mice, for thalamocortical (Rah et al., 2013) and hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapses (Druckmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Input clustering has been shown for hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapses in mice.
source: Input clustering has been shown for axodendritic contacts in the barn owl auditory system (McBride et al., 2008), and more recently, in mice, for thalamocortical (Rah et al., 2013) and hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapses (Druckmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In previous cases of reported clustering, there is no quantification of cluster parameters.
source: In all of these cases however there is no quantification of cluster parameters, which is crucial if one wants to relate the findings to any kind of biophysical model of dendritic computation.
evidence: This is an assertion about the limitations of previous studies.

claim: Quantification of cluster parameters is crucial if one wants to relate the findings to any kind of biophysical model of dendritic computation.
source: In all of these cases however there is no quantification of cluster parameters, which is crucial if one wants to relate the findings to any kind of biophysical model of dendritic computation.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the importance of quantification for modeling.

claim: The data and analysis go considerably beyond previous reports by identifying individual clusters and quantifying cluster parameters.
source: In this way our data and analysis go considerably beyond these reports by identifying individual clusters and quantifying cluster parameters, such as for example the number of inputs per cluster.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty and contribution of the current study.

claim: The novel method for spatial cluster analysis by combinatorial statistics can be applied to characterize any distribution or pattern of synapses on the postsynaptic dendrite.
source: Our novel method for spatial cluster analysis by combinatorial statistics is not limited to the synaptic connections described here. It can be applied to characterize any distribution or pattern of synapses on the postsynaptic dendrite as obtained for example by large scale electron microscopy, GFP reconstitution across synaptic partners, array tomography or mapping of synaptic activity (e.g Bock et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011; Druckmann et al., 2014; Kleindienst et al., 2011; Rah et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2012), as well as any other data regarding the spatial organization of structures along a one dimensional axis like for example the distribution of presynaptic boutons along an axon (e.g. Schuemann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the method, supported by citations to various techniques.

claim: The clusters of intracortical connections between L5 pyramidal neurons contain 4 to 14 synapses within 30 µm of basal dendrite.
source: Our results show that the clusters of intracortical connections between L5 pyramidal neurons contain 4 to 14 synapses within 30 µm of basal dendrite.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative results from the study.

claim: According to the known rules of dendritic integration and the spatiotemporal arithmetic of synaptic summation, such clusters would result in superlinear dendritic integration during synchronous synaptic activity.
source: According to the known rules of dendritic integration and the spatiotemporal arithmetic of synaptic summation (Branco and Häusser, 2011; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Polsky et al., 2004) such clusters would result in superlinear dendritic integration during synchronous synaptic activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured cluster parameters and established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Superlinear integration can also occur without tight clustering.
source: Superlinear integration can also occur without tight clustering (Branco et al., 2010; Losonczy and Magee, 2006), but the specifics of the spatial input organization are expected to define how different temporal activity patterns determine the firing pattern of the postsynaptic cell.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The specifics of the spatial input organization are expected to define how different temporal activity patterns determine the firing pattern of the postsynaptic cell.
source: Superlinear integration can also occur without tight clustering (Branco et al., 2010; Losonczy and Magee, 2006), but the specifics of the spatial input organization are expected to define how different temporal activity patterns determine the firing pattern of the postsynaptic cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about dendritic integration.

claim: The results are well explained by local learning rules.
source: Our results are well explained by local learning rules, which may not only be involved in cluster formation but also support interactions among synapses in a cluster during synaptic plasticity events (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Harvey and Svoboda, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of cited literature on learning rules.

claim: The results are in line with observations of spatially clustered spontaneous activity of synapses during development.
source: They are also in line with observations of spatially clustered spontaneous activity of synapses during development (Kleindienst et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2012) and clustered spine formation and synaptic potentiation during learning and experience-dependent plasticity (Fu et al., 2012; Makino and Malinow, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The results are in line with observations of clustered spine formation and synaptic potentiation during learning and experience-dependent plasticity.
source: They are also in line with observations of spatially clustered spontaneous activity of synapses during development (Kleindienst et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2012) and clustered spine formation and synaptic potentiation during learning and experience-dependent plasticity (Fu et al., 2012; Makino and Malinow, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A further potential role of input clusters may be to overcome the stochasticity of neurotransmitter release and help to increase the reliability of synaptic transmission.
source: A further potential role of input clusters may be to overcome the stochasticity of neurotransmitter release and help to increase the reliability of synaptic transmission (Bagnall et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functional roles, supported by citation.

claim: Typically connections between L5 pyramidal cells consist of 4 to 8 synapses, which are distributed over different branches of the postsynaptic dendrite.
source: Typically connections between L5 pyramidal cells consist of 4 to 8 synapses, which are distributed over different branches of the postsynaptic dendrite (Deuchars et al., 1994; Markram et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The synapses within L5 input clusters most likely arise from a set of presynaptic neurons rather than a single one.
source: This suggests that the synapses within L5 input clusters most likely arise from a set of presynaptic neurons rather than a single one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the typical number of synapses per connection and the number of synapses in clusters.

claim: Synchronous activation of L5 inputs within a cluster is expected to occur during L5 network oscillations.
source: Nevertheless, synchronous activation of L5 inputs within a cluster is expected to occur during L5 network oscillations (e.g. Buffalo et al., 2011; Sun and Dan, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature about network oscillations.

claim: In anesthetized rats, L5 pyramidal cells in visual cortex receive synchronously oscillating excitatory inputs.
source: In anesthetized rats, L5 pyramidal cells in visual cortex receive synchronously oscillating excitatory inputs (Sun and Dan, 2009), which are thought to arise from rhythmically firing L5 pyramidal cells (Flint and Connors, 1996; Silva et al., 1991) within the network of L5 pyramidal cells (Markram, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Synchronously oscillating excitatory inputs are thought to arise from rhythmically firing L5 pyramidal cells within the network of L5 pyramidal cells.
source: In anesthetized rats, L5 pyramidal cells in visual cortex receive synchronously oscillating excitatory inputs (Sun and Dan, 2009), which are thought to arise from rhythmically firing L5 pyramidal cells (Flint and Connors, 1996; Silva et al., 1991) within the network of L5 pyramidal cells (Markram, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Similar oscillations in L5 have been observed in awake animals.
source: Similar oscillations in L5 have been observed in awake animals (e.g. Buffalo et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The results provide the first characterization of synapse clusters arising from an anatomically and genetically defined input on the dendritic tree of cortical pyramidal cells.
source: In conclusion, our results, to our knowledge, provide the first characterization of synapse clusters arising from an anatomically and genetically defined input on the dendritic tree of cortical pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty and contribution of the study.

claim: Quantitative analysis of the spatial organization of inputs together with the rules of dendritic integration and synaptic summation will allow working out the logical operations of neural computations at the cellular level.
source: Only such quantitative analysis of the spatial organization of inputs together with the rules of dendritic integration and synaptic summation will allow working out the logical operations of neural computations at the cellular level, which are critical for understanding information processing in neural circuits.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of quantitative analysis for understanding neural computation.

claim: The logical operations of neural computations at the cellular level are critical for understanding information processing in neural circuits.
source: Only such quantitative analysis of the spatial organization of inputs together with the rules of dendritic integration and synaptic summation will allow working out the logical operations of neural computations at the cellular level, which are critical for understanding information processing in neural circuits.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of cellular-level computations for circuit function.

claim: CASIM has the advantage over other methods for mapping synapses that it identifies synapses in functional rather than only in structural or molecular terms.
source: CASIM has the advantage over other methods for mapping synapses by light or electron microscopy (e.g. Druckmann et al., 2014; Rah et al., 2013) that it identifies synapses in functional rather than only in structural or molecular terms.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the CASIM method compared to other approaches.

claim: Expression levels and stimulus sensitivity of ChR2 were different from cell to cell.
source: Expression levels and stimulus sensitivity were different from cell to cell.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: In more sensitive cells the number of generated action potentials dropped with higher stimulus intensities.
source: Because in more sensitive cells the number of generated action potentials dropped with higher stimulus intensities, we applied an intermediate stimulus intensity for synapse mapping, which evoked action potentials in 58% of L5 pyramidal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments that informed the choice of stimulus intensity.

claim: Layer 5 pyramidal cells with no detectable ChR2-YFP fluorescence were selected for synapse mapping.
source: For synapse mapping we selected layer 5 pyramidal cells with no detectable ChR2-YFP fluorescence, indicating that the levels of ChR2 expression are so low that the selected stimulus intensity is insufficient to cause significant depolarization.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell selection criteria.

claim: Due to the stochastic nature of neurotransmitter release, it is not expected that each AP leads to transmitter release.
source: Due to the stochastic nature of neurotransmitter release, it is not expected that each AP leads to transmitter release.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about synaptic transmission.

claim: Spines were classified as receiving L5 input if they displayed at least once a higher (≥3×standard deviation) and earlier peak calcium signal evoked by photostimulation than observed in the parent dendrite.
source: Thus we classified spines as receiving L5 input if they displayed at least once a higher (≥3×standard deviation) and earlier peak calcium signal evoked by photostimulation than observed in the parent dendrite (Figure 1D - 1G).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the classification criteria.

claim: In adulthood the occurrence of 'silent' synapses is effectively negligible.
source: Since in adulthood the occurrence of 'silent' synapses is effectively negligible (Rumpel et al., 1998) NMDA receptor mediated calcium signals are expected to identify functional synapses containing both AMPA and NMDA receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NMDA receptor mediated calcium signals are expected to identify functional synapses containing both AMPA and NMDA receptors.
source: Since in adulthood the occurrence of 'silent' synapses is effectively negligible (Rumpel et al., 1998) NMDA receptor mediated calcium signals are expected to identify functional synapses containing both AMPA and NMDA receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about silent synapses.

claim: The photostimulus evoked on average 1.57 ± 0.54 (n = 12) action potentials selectively in 58% of the ChR2 expressing L5 neurons.
source: The photostimulus (470 nm LED; Rapp OptoElectronic GmbH, Wedel, Germany) consisted of 3 pulses of 2 ms at 30 Hz (4 mW at the objective back-aperture) and was applied via the fluorescence excitation path of the microscope to the full field of view. It evoked on average 1.57 ± 0.54 (n = 12) action potentials selectively in 58% of the ChR2 expressing L5 neurons (Figure 1—figure supplements 1,2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments.

claim: The median nearest neighbor distance between L5+ spines from experiments (median = 3.10 μm) is significantly different from reshuffled data (median = 5.02 ± 0.43 μm; p<0.0001).
source: Median values of recorded and reshuffled data are significantly different (data, median = 3.10 μm; simulations, median = 5.02 ± 0.43 μm; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis comparing experimental data to simulations.

claim: The deviation between experimental and simulated inter-input distances is most pronounced for small inter-input distances below 10 µm with a peak deviation around 5 µm.
source: The plot of the difference between inter-input distances from experiments and simulations (purple) shows that the deviation is most pronounced for small inter-input distances below 10 µm with a peak deviation around 5 µm, suggesting a clustered arrangement of L5+ spines.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 45 input ensembles were found in 20 cells (total analyzed dendritic length 2718 μm).
source: We found 45 input ensembles in 20 cells (total analyzed dendritic length 2718 μm; Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, gray boxes).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cluster analysis.

claim: The mean specific ensemble likelihood of the 12 identified clusters is 0.003 ± 0.0008.
source: Defining ensembles of at least three inputs with a likelihood ≤1% as cluster, we classified 12 out of 45 ensembles as clusters (mean specific ensemble likelihood=0.003 ± 0.0008; Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, red asterisks).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cluster analysis.

claim: The probability to observe 11 segments with a cluster has a P value below 0.001.
source: We find that the probability to observe c segments containing a cluster in the data set of 40 segments in total declines and remains below the significance threshold of 0.001 until the second last of the sorted segments (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis.

claim: The number of 11 segments with a cluster with a P value below 0.001 supports the hypothesis that L5+ spines are indeed arranged in clusters not by chance.
source: However, the number of 11 segments with a cluster with a P value below 0.001 supports the hypothesis that L5+ spines are indeed arranged in clusters not by chance.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis results.

claim: The fraction of remaining L5 pyramidal cell axon density that can be activated in a slice is between 50% and 70% depending on the depth in the slice.
source: From this we estimate that the fraction of the remaining L5 pyramidal cell axon density that can be activated in a slice is between 50% and 70% depending on the depth in the slice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is an estimation based on calculations described in the methods.

claim: Between 30% and 50% of L5 inputs are missed due to the slicing process.
source: This suggests that between 30% and 50% of L5 inputs are missed due to the slicing process.
evidence: This is an inference from the calculation of remaining axon density.

claim: The total discrepancy between manual verification and the classification by the algorithm was 2.37% in individual traces.
source: In the individual traces (n = 15293 acquisitions), the total discrepancy between manual verification and the classification by the algorithm was 2.37%, which translated into a total discrepancy of 6.46% with respect to the input classification (0.55% false negatives, 4.2% false positives, 1.71% ambiguous; n = 2168 spines).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of the accuracy of the classification algorithm.

claim: The total discrepancy with respect to the input classification was 6.46% (0.55% false negatives, 4.2% false positives, 1.71% ambiguous; n = 2168 spines).
source: In the individual traces (n = 15293 acquisitions), the total discrepancy between manual verification and the classification by the algorithm was 2.37%, which translated into a total discrepancy of 6.46% with respect to the input classification (0.55% false negatives, 4.2% false positives, 1.71% ambiguous; n = 2168 spines).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of the accuracy of the classification algorithm.

claim: CASIM might miss synapses with very low release probability.
source: CASIM might miss synapses with very low release probability but otherwise the false negative rate is mostly determined by the fraction of presynaptic neurons not expressing ChR2 as with other approaches relying on the expression of markers of any kind (e.g. Druckmann et al., 2014; Rah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about a potential limitation of the method.

claim: The false negative rate is mostly determined by the fraction of presynaptic neurons not expressing ChR2.
source: CASIM might miss synapses with very low release probability but otherwise the false negative rate is mostly determined by the fraction of presynaptic neurons not expressing ChR2 as with other approaches relying on the expression of markers of any kind (e.g. Druckmann et al., 2014; Rah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference about the main source of false negatives, with comparison to other methods.

claim: Undersampling the presynaptic population is expected to be random and would not introduce artifacts of non-random structure in the mapped synapse distribution.
